name: Shingles
definition: Shingles is a painful rash caused by the chickenpox virus becoming active again after lying dormant in the body.
overview: Shingles comes from the same virus that causes chickenpox, which stays dormant in the body and can reactivate later. The NHS describes tingling or pain in an area of skin as an early sign, followed by a rash on one side of the body. The CDC adds that some people also have fatigue, fever or headache. The NHS says the rash can take up to 4 weeks to heal, and pain can last longer.
causes: Reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus, which causes chickenpox and stays dormant in the body afterwards
riskFactors: Older age: the CDC says the risk of shingles and its complications rises sharply after 50 years of age
A weakened immune system, which the CDC links to a higher risk of shingles and its complications
signs: A rash on one side of the body, with itchy blisters that later dry and scab
In some people the rash is in and around the eye, which can affect sight
complications: Long-lasting nerve pain after the rash (postherpetic neuralgia)
Infection of the rash and scarring
Ramsay Hunt syndrome, a rare complication affecting the facial nerve
diagnosis: A clinician can usually diagnose shingles from the rash itself. The CDC notes it can be harder to recognise in children and younger adults when the rash is mild.
treatment: The CDC says there is no cure, but antiviral medicine can help, and pain relief medicine can also be used. The NHS says mild cases may need no treatment, and antiviral tablets may be offered for a weakened immune system, moderate or severe pain, or a rash spreading beyond the chest, tummy and back. Antivirals usually need to be started within 3 days of the rash first appearing, according to the NHS.
prevention: The CDC says vaccination lowers the chance of shingles and makes it milder if it still occurs. UKHSA says the national programme uses Shingrix, a two-dose vaccine.
seekCare: The NHS says an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111 is the route if shingles is suspected and the person is pregnant, has a rash on the eye or nose, has changes to vision, or has a severely weakened immune system. For other suspected cases, the NHS says a pharmacist or GP can help, and antivirals work best started within about 3 days of the rash appearing. In the UK, sudden severe symptoms or collapse are a 999 emergency.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of shingles and how is it diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS describes the first signs as a tingling or painful feeling in an area of skin, sometimes with a headache or feeling generally unwell. A rash then follows, usually on one side of the body. The CDC says the rash is most often painful, itchy or tingly, and the NHS describes itchy blisters that later dry and scab. Some people also have general symptoms of a viral infection, such as fatigue, fever or headache.

NHS Wales says the rash can sit in and around the eye and can affect sight or hearing. A clinician can usually diagnose shingles from the rash itself, according to the CDC. A clinical review notes that unusual presentations can make the diagnosis challenging in some people. The CDC adds that diagnosis can be harder in children and younger adults, especially when the illness is mild.

sections.heading: What causes shingles, and can it spread to other people?
sections.body:
Shingles is caused by varicella-zoster virus, the virus behind chickenpox. After chickenpox, the virus stays dormant in the body and can reactivate later. The CDC says the risk of shingles rises sharply after 50 years of age, and that people with weakened immune systems also have a higher risk. NHS Wales says a person cannot get shingles from someone who has shingles or chickenpox.

The NHS says shingles itself cannot be passed on, but a person who has never had chickenpox or the chickenpox vaccine could catch chickenpox from someone with shingles. The CDC says exposure is through direct contact with fluid from the blisters, and NHS Wales says a person is infectious to others only while the rash is weeping fluid. The NHS names pregnant women who have not had chickenpox, people with weakened immune systems and babies under 1 month old as groups to avoid contact with.

sections.heading: How is shingles treated, and how long does it take to heal?
sections.body:
The CDC says there is no cure for shingles, but antiviral medicine can help. Early treatment can reduce or prevent severe pain and help blisters dry faster, according to the CDC. The NHS says mild cases may need no treatment, while antiviral tablets may be offered for a weakened immune system, moderate or severe pain, or a rash spreading beyond the chest, tummy and back. These medicines usually need to be started within 3 days of the rash first appearing, and the NHS says pharmacists can supply the same antivirals as GPs. Pain relief medicine can also help, the CDC says.

A clinical review lists topical treatments, anticonvulsants, antidepressants and, in severe cases, opioids among the options for pain during an outbreak. The NHS says the rash can take up to 4 weeks to heal, and that pain can persist afterwards but usually improves over time. NICE guidance on nerve pain says referral to a specialist pain service can be considered at any stage. CKS says clinical judgement guides management in people who are immunosuppressed.

sections.heading: What complications can shingles cause, and when is urgent help needed?
sections.body:
The CDC says the most common complication is postherpetic neuralgia, a long-lasting nerve pain. The NHS also lists infection of the rash, scarring, muscle weakness and eye problems. The CDC adds hearing or vision loss and encephalitis. The NHS says Ramsay Hunt syndrome, which affects the facial nerve, is a rare complication. If the cornea is involved, the CDC says treatment to avert permanent scarring is important for preventing lasting vision loss.

The CDC advises urgent care for eye symptoms and immediate medical evaluation for neurological symptoms away from the area of the rash. The NHS says an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is the route when shingles is suspected and the person is pregnant, has a rash on the eye or nose, has changes to vision, or has a severely weakened immune system. For other suspected cases, a pharmacist or GP appointment is the usual route, because antivirals work best when started within about 3 days. In the UK, sudden severe symptoms or collapse call for 999.

sections.heading: Can a vaccine prevent shingles?
sections.body:
The CDC says vaccination lowers the chance of shingles and makes it milder if it still occurs. The CDC recommends 2 doses of recombinant zoster vaccine, known as Shingrix, for adults aged 50 years and older. It also recommends the vaccine for some younger adults with weakened immune systems. UKHSA says the UK programme now uses only Shingrix, a two-dose vaccine, because the older Zostavax vaccine has been withdrawn.

The NHS says the vaccine is available to people who turned 65 on or after 1 September 2023, to unvaccinated people aged 70 to 79, and to people aged 50 and over with a severely weakened immune system. UKHSA says eligibility for the immunocompetent is phased in by age, and from 1 September 2025 extends to severely immunosuppressed adults aged 18 and over. Eligibility can change over time, so the NHS page is the reference for current rules.

faqs.a: The CDC says there is no cure for shingles, but antiviral medicine can help. Early treatment can reduce or prevent severe pain and help blisters dry faster. The NHS says antivirals usually need to start within 3 days of the rash appearing, and that the rash can take up to 4 weeks to heal.

The NHS says shingles itself cannot be passed on. However, someone who has never had chickenpox or the chickenpox vaccine could catch chickenpox from a person with shingles. The CDC says exposure is through direct contact with fluid from the blisters. NHS Wales says a person is infectious only while the rash is weeping fluid.

faqs.q: Who is more likely to get shingles?
faqs.a: The CDC says the risk of shingles and its complications rises sharply after 50 years of age. People with weakened immune systems also have a higher risk of shingles and of complications, according to the CDC. In the US, the CDC recommends two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine for adults aged 50 and over.

The CDC describes postherpetic neuralgia as a long-lasting nerve pain and the most common complication of shingles. The NHS says pain can persist after the rash heals but usually improves over time. NICE guidance on nerve pain says referral to a specialist pain service can be considered at any stage.

faqs.q: What does the NHS say about shingles in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says shingles in pregnancy is usually mild, and a GP arranges specialist advice on whether treatment is needed. Pregnancy is also listed as a reason to ask for an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111 when shingles is suspected. The NHS also names pregnant women who have not had chickenpox as a group to avoid contact with.
